title: Large populations favour natural selection by supplying more variations

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Large populations favour natural selection by supplying more variations

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: A large number of individuals favours natural selection because it gives a better chance for profitable variations to arise within a given period, compensating for lower variability in each individual.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: A large number of individuals, by giving a better chance for the appearance within any given period of profitable variations, will compensate for a lesser amount of variability in each individual, and is, I believe, an extremely important element of success.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter IV, “Natural Selection”; section “Circumstances favourable and unfavourable to Natural Selection, namely, intercrossing, isolation, number of individuals”. Scope: all species undergoing natural selection

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch04-14: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.63

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Population genetics provides explicit quantities and experimental datasets can discriminate the mechanism. Natural-population data linking population size to the arrival of beneficial variation remain limited.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Across populations differing in census and effective size, compare the supply and establishment rate of beneficial mutations while controlling mutation rate and environment. A positive population-size effect on beneficial-variant appearance and adaptation rate supports the mechanism.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Clonal interference and drift can make adaptation rate non-monotonic.

Census size, effective size and mutation supply differ.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.79
data existence: 0.64
analysis feasibility: 0.61
discriminating power: 0.62
data adequacy: 0.46

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Population size and adaptive rate are measurable, and genomic plus abundance datasets support a comparative regression for vertebrates and a few other groups. That is a subset of all species under selection, and Ne is inferred rather than counted. The regression is informative but confounded by life history, so it tests the abundance effect only partially.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Relate the rate of adaptive substitution, or additive genetic variance for fitness, to effective or census population size across species. A positive partial relationship would confirm that larger populations supply more usable variation per unit time; no relationship after mutation rate and life history are controlled would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Effective population size is estimated for far fewer species than the claim covers.

Census sizes on the Red List are coarse and taxonomically biased.

Life history and mutation rate covary with abundance and also change substitution rates.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.4
analysis feasibility: 0.58
data existence: 0.66
operationalizability: 0.68
discriminating power: 0.52
